key_insight: You can estimate the expected output of a wide, randomly initialized MLP on Gaussian inputs analytically — without Monte Carlo — by approximating layerwise activation distributions and propagating them through the network.
problem_solved: Sampling-based estimation of expected outputs or losses is costly and noisy; the paper removes the need to run many forward samples at initialization while retaining accurate expectations.
method: Represent layer activations using low-order statistics (cumulants/moments) to form compact approximate distributions.
Propagate these distributions through nonlinearities using Hermite-polynomial (orthogonal expansion) techniques to update cumulants across layers.
Evaluate the network's expected output analytically from the final activation approximation, avoiding sample-based forward passes.
impact: Provides a fast, low-variance alternative to Monte Carlo for estimating expectations at initialization, enabling cheaper analysis of architectures and initializations and accelerating research tasks that require many expectation evaluations.
visual_elements: Side-by-side diagram: Monte Carlo pipeline (many sampled forwards) vs analytic pipeline (cumulant/Hermite propagation) with compute/time icons

Plot: estimation error vs compute/time comparing analytic method and Monte Carlo across sample counts

paper_title: Estimating the expected output of wide random MLPs more efficiently than sampling
paper_authors: Wilson Wu, Victor Lecomte, Michael Winer, George Robinson, Jacob Hilton
